Declined rather than deleted: an item that was planned and reorganised is a different fact from one that was never planned.

items.title: The cross-revision regression report

items.done_when: The v14.36 to v15.0 headline reproduces from the real archives and names lost content by identity, not by count. If it does not, the archaeology is wrong.

items.title: nomos-capability: the contract registry whose answer is never a bare no
items.why: A capability nobody registered must answer Unknown, not No. Collapsing those is how 'we cannot tell whether this rule applies' becomes 'this rule does not apply', which is the same defect as a validator that never ran. items.done_when: An unregistered capability yields Unknown and a registered-but-unavailable one yields a distinct answer naming why. A test asserts the two are not the same value and that no code path turns either into a grant.

items.title: nomos-analysis: FactIdentity, FactReader, FactStore and invalidation
items.why: The load-bearing architectural bet, still untested. FactIdentity is the cache key AND the identity, one type, so a fact cannot be reused under a key that does not describe it. FactReader is the only read path and records a dependency edge on every read, which is what makes invalidation dependency-complete rather than hopeful.
items.done_when: A change in any one of FactIdentity's components invalidates, asserted component by component rather than in aggregate. Require() returns the honest degraded Applicability on failure and never a fabricated fact. Reading through FactReader records an edge; a test proves a read that recorded no edge is not possible.

items.title: A fact's identity stops naming a workspace state
items.why: FactKey carries a SnapshotId, and a workspace snapshot is a digest over every member. A fact key that names one therefore changes for every fact in the corpus when any one file is edited: over the six-file precision corpus, editing alpha/one.rs recomputed eight facts where two changed, and at corpus scale that is 9,440 per keystroke. Two components already answer what the snapshot is there for and answer them finer — semantic_inputs says what a fact was computed from, and the generation says which state it is current at. The snapshot is a third answer, it is the coarsest, and it erases both. OD-ANALYSIS-001 records the measurement; tests/integration works around it by pinning, which is why the component currently does no work at all.
items.done_when: FactKey no longer carries a snapshot, and a fact's relation to a workspace state is provenance on MaterializedFact rather than part of what the fact is. GenerationCause::SnapshotReplaced is re-expressed in terms a caller replacing a snapshot actually has — the members that differ — rather than by matching a key component that no longer exists. Component::All and the test that walks every key component agree with the new shape. tests/integration stops pinning: Slice takes the workspace's current snapshot, and the exact-descendants assertion still names exactly two facts. OD-ANALYSIS-001 is closed with what decided it.

items.title: Which of several usable offers wins
items.why: Registry::Resolve picks the first usable offer in provider-name order. With one provider that was invisible; with two it means a caller that lowers its floor to Approximate — to get an answer for the 7 files a parser refuses — is served the scanner for all 7,580, including the 7,573 the parser would have read exactly, and is told Supported. Strongest-wins is the reflex answer and is not free: a Guarantee says how good an answer is and nothing about what it costs, so always reaching for the strongest turns 'I will accept an approximation' into 'give me the best you have'. OD-CAPABILITY-001 states the three candidates and why none is obvious.
items.done_when: Selection among usable offers is decided rather than incidental: Registry::Resolve applies a stated rule, the rule is named in the type or documented at the method with what decided it, and renaming a provider cannot change which one answers. A caller that would have been served a weaker offer than one available can tell — either by the rule making that impossible or by the resolution saying so. OD-CAPABILITY-001 is closed with what decided it, and tests/integration's assertion of the current name-order behaviour is replaced by an assertion of the new rule.

items.title: A skipped test must not report ok
items.why: Measured: 697 tests pass with no corpus configured, and 68 of them are corpus-gated — they return early and print ok having read nothing. CI (.github/workflows/gate.yml) sets none of NOMOS_V14_CORPUS, NOMOS_SPEC_ARCHIVES or NOMOS_RUST_CORPUS, so the normalizer reproduction, the byte order mark sweep, the 282/258 and 30/28 counts, restoration, the family counts and the ingestion-order determinism claim are all reporting ok on every pull request without touching their subject. Misconfiguration is already loud — every helper asserts root.is_dir() with the reasoning written at the assertion — so the defect is absence, not error. This is exactly what Test_The_Workspace_Should_Not_Appear_Empty exists to prevent one level up: a check that cannot find its subject must fail loudly rather than quietly verify nothing. The repository states the rule and does not apply it to its own gating.
items.done_when: The set of corpus-gated tests is declared in one place and checked against the source, so a test cannot become gated without appearing in the declaration and a declaration cannot name a test that no longer gates. The three corpus variables are documented together with what each one covers and how many assertions it carries. A run without a corpus reports the count of what it did not check, in a form CI surfaces, rather than leaving 68 ok lines to speak for it. The count is measured rather than estimated, and changing it fails.

items.title: Four phases of specification system with no way to read it
items.why: nomos has exactly one group: work. Phase 2's stated day-one payoff — ask what the canonical domain model said, verbatim, and get the real rows — is still not answerable from a command line, and Phase 4 shipped fourteen projection profiles and renderers with no command that runs one. The gap was flagged closing P2-BUNDLE and is further away now, because there is more behind it. It also compounds P9-SKIP: the store is built from a corpus that lives outside this repository, so a read command is only as reachable as the corpus, and that has to be said rather than discovered.
items.done_when: A group on the nomos binary answers the query Phase 2 named — a record or table read out verbatim by identifier — and renders at least one Phase 4 profile to a file. A missing or unreadable corpus is reported as an absence with what was expected, never as an empty result. The commands are exercised by a test that runs the built binary rather than calling the library, because the argument parsing is the part that has never run.

items.title: Nothing walks the selection the floor bought
items.why: P8-SELECTION made Selection::Weaker reachable and nothing spends it. A caller lowers its floor to Approximate because a parser refuses seven files, the registry hands back the parser and the scanner in order, and Slice::Dispatch asks the parser and degrades the run on refusal — so the coverage the floor admitted is available and unused. The prior question is not the dispatch loop: a FactKey names the provider that answered, so per-subject fallback files one capability's facts under two providers within one run. Whether that is a coherent store or two answers to one question under one address is a decision, and it has to be reached before the loop is written.
items.done_when: The decision is recorded first, against a stated criterion. Then either the run walks the selection per subject — with the store still single-valued for what a file declares at a given generation, and RunReport naming which provider answered for how many subjects — or a record states why per-subject fallback is refused and what a caller should do instead. A negative control confirmed red either way: with fallback, a run where the strong provider refuses must not report the corpus clean.

items.title: The markdown round trip D-129 decided and nobody built
items.why: D-129 is a governing record, accepted, in the store, and it says markdown remains the surface people author through via a round trip that reads a record out as markdown and writes the edit back, as a transaction against the store: claim, stage, preview, commit, with the preview mandatory. None of that exists. Nothing reads a record out and nothing writes one back. Amended at version 2 to say so, which makes the gap schedulable and does not close it. What follows is the part that matters: records under docs/records are still the substrate in practice — authored as files, seeded into the store from those files by include_str!, edited as files — so the store holds a copy and the direction of that dependency is the opposite of what D-129 decides.
items.done_when: A record can be read out of the store as markdown byte-identical to what would be seeded from it, and an edit to that markdown can be written back as a transaction that previews what it changes before committing. Identity survives the round trip: the node_id, the blocks and the relations are the same afterwards, and a rename is an ordinary edit. The preview names whether normative wording moved, because D-129 calls that mandatory and a preview that cannot say it is not the preview the record decided. Either docs/records stops being the authoring substrate, or a record states why it remains one and D-129 is amended again to agree with the tree.

items.title: An item's verification is weaker than the gate it stands in for
items.why: work finish runs the item's argv and records the item done if it exits zero. Every item's argv is a cargo test invocation. The gate in .github/workflows/gate.yml is clippy with -D warnings and then cargo test, and the workspace denies unwrap_used, indexing_slicing and arithmetic_side_effects — a panic on the analysis path is a determinism defect rather than a bug, which is why they deny. So an item can be recorded verified while the gate that follows it is red. That is not hypothetical: P9-SKIP and P9-PHASE-GAP were both recorded verified with a clippy error in a file the item had just written, caught by running clippy by hand afterwards. Twice in three items, by somebody being careful — which is the arrangement the ledger exists to stop relying on, and the same sentence OD-LEDGER-001 already had to write once.
items.done_when: An item cannot be finished by a predicate that checks less than the gate does. Either finish refuses an argv that does not cover the gate, or the ledger derives the predicate rather than taking it from the author, or a record states why a weaker predicate is right and what the author is expected to run instead. Whichever is chosen, the two instances above would have failed under it, and a test says so.

items.title: work list calls an item ready when nothing can claim it
items.why: This item was authored on a false premise and is rewritten rather than deleted, because the premise is the interesting part. It said depends_on is unenforced. It is enforced: Claim walks the item's dependencies and returns ClaimRefusal::DependencyUnmet, retryable, exit 3. Verified against the case the item cites — `work claim --item P9-README` answers `refused: P9-README depends on P9-READ-SURFACE, which is Claimed`. The defect is one layer out. `work list` reads the item's state field, which is Ready, and prints the same word it prints for an item anybody can take. An agent picking work off that column burns a round trip per blocked item and learns to distrust the column. Whoever takes this must not add a second enforcement: two guards for one rule is how they come to disagree.
items.done_when: work list distinguishes an item whose dependencies are unfinished from one that is claimable, without consulting a second source of truth about what blocks a claim. A test covers it over an item with an unfinished dependency, and a negative control covers one with none, so the new label cannot be printed for everything. Claim's refusal is unchanged and still tested.

items.why: Three completeness checks in this workspace compared one side against the other and never the reverse, and all three were found by accident. Assert_Complete in nomos-spec-bundle counts every row in the store against every record in the bundle, and a new column exported cleanly until Assert_Columns_Covered was written as its mirror. Import needed the same treatment: Assert_Landed documents itself as "the mirror of the exporter completeness guard". GOVERNING_RECORD_IDS was compared against a seeded store and never against docs/records, so six governing records - among them OD-STORE-001 and OD-ANALYSIS-001, which decide how the store and the analysis kernel behave - declared canonical-normative authority, were cited in commits and in other records, and never reached the store. The test that closed it, Test_Every_Canonical_Record_On_Disk_Should_Be_Governing, calls itself "the direction nothing checked" in its own doc comment. Each instance was repaired where it was found and the shape was never named, so the fourth one is unguarded and the third was found by hunting rather than by looking it up. That is the argument OD-LEDGER-001 already had to make once and P9-PREDICATE is making again: a defect caught by somebody being careful is not caught.
items.done_when: The rule is written down and enforced rather than remembered. A record names the shape - a completeness assertion compares two sets, and asserting one containment is half a check - and something fails when a one-directional completeness check is added, rather than a reviewer noticing. Enumerating the completeness assertions the workspace already has, each paired with its mirror, is part of the answer and not a substitute for it. Whichever form the enforcement takes, all three instances above would have failed it as originally written, and a test says so.

items.title: The enforcement module is declared in full and implemented by nothing
items.why: Measured against the tree rather than the plan: ten public types in nomos-contracts are referenced by no file outside that crate, and four of them - GateCategory, EnforcerRef, EnforcementBreach, EnforcementReach - are the whole of enforcement.rs. It is the only module in that crate that is wholly unimplemented; every other family has consumers, including the four determinism types, which acquired theirs while this item was being written. What enforcement.rs describes is what the plan calls Phase 8: a rules engine, findings, gates, and the commands nomos check and nomos gate. None of the named crates is a workspace member and the binary has two groups, work and spec. A schema is not a feature is this project own rule, and nomos-contracts is the crate whose every type is reimplemented by peers that will never compile it, so a declaration there with no implementation is a published protocol commitment accruing cost. OD-LEDGER-002 recorded the numbering half of this and deliberately opened no item for the work. The wider fact is that nothing in this tree has yet judged anyone code: P8 was six follow-ups to P7, P9 is nine findings against P8 and the tree, and two consecutive batches have produced correction and audit rather than capability.
items.done_when: One rule runs end to end and judges real code. It is reachable from the binary as a command rather than from a test only, it produces a typed Finding rather than a printed line, and the enforcement vocabulary it reports through is the one already declared in nomos-contracts rather than a second one invented next to it. A negative control is confirmed red: code that violates the rule must fail, and the test proving that must fail if the rule is weakened. The rule chosen is the completeness-mirror rule from P9-ONE-DIRECTION, because it is the one rule in this tree with three recorded instances and therefore three historical cases to test a judgment against. Scope is one rule, not three; a second rule is a later item, and this one is done when a single check is honest end to end.

items.title: Two rows of the determinism table are undeclared, and both are in crates/spec
items.why: P9-DETERMINISM declared four execution domains and checked each against behaviour. The domain table in nomos-contracts has six rows. The two it did not reach are spec-bundle serialization and the projection engine output, both in crates/spec, which that item did not claim and did not touch. The gap is currently a sentence in Test_The_Declared_Domains_Should_Be_The_Ones_This_Item_Covered and a paragraph in OD-DETERMINISM-001, which is better than silence and is not a schedule. The bundle row matters most. Its declared scope is CrossBinary, the strongest in the table, because a bundle is an interchange artefact read by a build that did not write it, and nothing has ever compared one across two builds.

The completeness guard is extended to reach domains that do not construct facts, so that the next undeclared row fails a test rather than being noticed - and it must fail if either new declaration is removed. items.title: Every item claims docs/records, so the ledger runs one item at a time
items.why: All eight open items on this ledger reserve docs/records. Not most - all of them, measured. So exactly one item can be held at a time, whatever else the ledger says about parallelism, and nomos-ledger opens by stating that territory-based exclusion exists "so that several agents can work one repository without silently overwriting each other". Observed three times in one afternoon on 2026-08-09: P9-DETERMINISM held, and all six Ready items refused; the same claim widened, still all six; then P9-ONE-DIRECTION held, and all seven remaining items refused - six on territory and the seventh on a dependency. Each time work list reported every one of them ready. The cause is not an authoring mistake. OD-LEDGER-001 second authoring rule says an item that will produce a decision claims docs/records, and any item whose why names an open question or a suspected defect will produce a record. On an audit ledger every item names a suspected defect, so the rule that was written to stop territory being under-declared now guarantees that every item excludes every other one. Two agents cannot work this repository concurrently by construction, and the mechanism reports that as a queue rather than as a design limit.
items.done_when: Two items that will each write a different record can be held at the same time. Whether that comes from an item claiming the record it will write rather than the directory the records live in, from a finer resolution over that path, or from an authoring rule that stops sending every item to one directory, the check is the same: with two such items on the ledger both claims are granted, and a test asserts it over the case that exists right now. Amending OD-LEDGER-001 second authoring rule is part of the answer rather than a separate item, because that rule is what produces the collision. A negative control confirms that two items which genuinely would write the same record are still refused, so the fix cannot be a blanket exemption for docs/records.

items.title: Abandoning an item destroys more of the record than crashing does
items.why: Measured against the code rather than the commit message that noticed it. nomos work abandon requires --reason and the ledger drops it. ReleaseOutcome::Abandoned carries reason: String non-optionally, which is the same technique the doc comment on ReleaseOutcome praises for the finished arm - carrying the evidence in the signature so that a release cannot express itself without one. The store then destructures it away: in Release, the Finished arm writes verified = Some(record) and the Abandoned arm is a `{ .. }` pattern that sets state = Ready and nothing else. Adjacent arms of one match, one persisting its evidence and one discarding it. The claim goes to None, the item goes back to Ready, and afterwards nothing on the item says it was ever held. The one reason this ledger does persist belongs to ItemState::Declined, where the doc comment says it is carried in the variant so an item cannot be declined reasonlessly - and it survives because it is part of the state rather than part of the transition. That is the structural line: a reason attached to a state is kept, a reason attached to a transition is not, and only one of the two is enforced at the type level. The consequence inverts the crate own stated intent. item.rs says a lapsed claim does not release itself, and stays visible so that a person can see the work was abandoned rather than never started. So an agent that dies holding a claim leaves a visible record, and an agent that abandons deliberately, having been made to write down why, leaves none. The well-behaved path is the lossy one. Observed on 2026-08-09 releasing P9-ONE-DIRECTION: the reason given said where the work had got to and why it stopped, and it survives only in the message of commit a749f9a, which is the half-recorded shape OD-SPEC-005 and commit 20296d9 both exist to name.
items.done_when: An abandonment is readable from the ledger after the fact. The reason the holder gave, who gave it, and when, survive on the item that was abandoned, and are reachable through the surface that reports an item rather than only by reading the file. A test asserts this over a claim-then-abandon cycle. The negative control is confirmed red: the test must fail when the abandoned arm goes back to discarding the reason, which means asserting the stored text itself and not merely that a field is present. A second control holds the line the crate already draws - abandoning must still return the item to Ready and still clear the claim, because a record of an abandonment must not go on excluding anyone. Whether a lapsed claim is owed the same treatment, which the crate deliberately leaves visible and for which nobody writes a reason, is settled either way in the record rather than left open.

items.title: A loud predicate is recorded as no verdict, because nothing drains its pipe
items.why: StdProcessLauncher pipes a predicate stdout and stderr and reads neither until after the child has exited. The wait loop calls try_wait, sleeps, and never drains. A child that writes past the pipe buffer blocks on the write, never exits, and is killed at the timeout, so a predicate that passed is recorded as no verdict at all. Demonstrated on a scratch ledger on 2026-08-09, same program and same 60 second timeout, only the volume changed: 840,000 bytes emitted in one second timed out after 60 seconds, and 4,000 bytes emitted the same way verified in zero. Met for real while finishing P10-FIRST-CHECK, whose predicate is cargo test --workspace: 75,751 bytes of output, 103 seconds by hand, TimedOut twice at 600 seconds under work finish. Every earlier item on this ledger scoped its predicate to one or two crates and stayed under the buffer, which is why four phases of work never met this. The consequence is the one shape this repository keeps recording. P9-PREDICATE separated GateFailed from PredicateFailed because a failing gate and failing work are different facts, and NoVerdict was added so that nobody found out could not read as bad work. This defect turns the failure direction into a lie in the other direction: a run that did find out, and found nothing wrong, is written down as nobody found out. Worse for a failing run, where the failure detail is exactly what makes the output large: the louder the failure, the more likely it is reported as a timeout rather than as a failure.
items.done_when: A predicate that writes more than the pipe buffer is verified on its result rather than killed on its volume. The check is a test in nomos-platform-std that runs a program emitting several hundred kilobytes quickly under a short timeout and asserts ExitOutcome::Exited with the real code, which fails against todays launcher. Both negative controls hold: a program that genuinely exceeds its timeout must still report TimedOut, and the captured output must still be the program actual output rather than a truncated prefix that happens to fit. Whether the fix drains on threads, uses a growing buffer, or moves to a platform crate that already solves it is open. Once it lands, P10-FIRST-CHECK predicate can drop the -q it carries only to fit the buffer, and the ledger recorded evidence for that item stops being a run of empty doctest sections.

items.title: Two guards disagree about whether DECLARED_RULES is mirrored
items.why:
nomos check and the contract test table give different answers to the same question about the same universe, and one of the two is a false claim of coverage. mirror.rs judges a declared universe by the mirror it names at the site, in its doc comment, and resolves that name against real parsed test functions. DECLARED_RULES in crates/spec/nomos-spec-validate/src/run.rs names none, so nomos check reports it as an admitted gap: declares no mirror, Advisory. The UNIVERSES table in tests/contract/tests/completeness_universes.rs classifies that same constant as Standing::Mirrored by Test_A_Rule_Nobody_Declared_Should_Fail_The_Run. The arithmetic isolates the disagreement exactly. Sixteen declared universes; the table calls four mirrored and twelve unmirrored, with UNMIRRORED_TOTAL at 12; nomos check finds thirteen unmirrored; the single difference between the two sets is DECLARED_RULES. The module documentation at the top of mirror.rs says thirteen, twice, so the rule and its own prose already disagree with the table.
The table is the one that is wrong, and it is worth saying why rather than which. Test_A_Rule_Nobody_Declared_Should_Fail_The_Run builds a synthetic Fake carrying the invented id NSV-INVENTED-001 and asserts that Validate reports it undeclared. It exercises the reconciliation mechanism against input the test made up. It never compares DECLARED_RULES against the rules this crate actually implements, and nothing else does either. Registered() in preserve.rs is a second hand-written list of the same four rules, and Validate reconciles the two hand-written lists against one another, which is precisely what makes the pair look covered: two lists agreeing catch a disagreement between two hands, never a divergence from the code. A fifth impl Rule added to preserve.rs and left out of Registered() is absent from both lists, is never run, and is reported by nothing. That it is invisible even to the scanner is a second fact: Read_Universes does not recognize a function returning Vec<Box<dyn Rule>> as a universe at all, so the list that enumerates the real thing is not judged by the rule that judges lists.
The severity ordering mirror.rs sets for itself is what makes this an item rather than a footnote. A phantom mirror is Blocking and an admitted gap is only Advisory, because a false claim of coverage is worse than a hole somebody wrote down and counted. This claim escapes that ordering only by being written in a hand-maintained table in another file, where the rule that judges coverage claims cannot resolve it. The three instances OD-COMPLETENESS-001 analyses were each repaired by naming the mirror at the site, which is why nomos check reports none of them; DECLARED_RULES is the one row the table calls mirrored that did not follow that convention. Noticed while finishing P10-FIRST-CHECK and recorded until now only in the Consequences section of D-134, which is the half-recorded shape OD-SPEC-005 exists to name.
items.done_when: The two guards agree about DECLARED_RULES, and the agreement is checked rather than asserted once by hand. Either DECLARED_RULES gets a real mirror - a check comparing it against the rules the crate actually implements rather than against a second hand-written list, named at the site so that nomos check resolves it - or the table admits the gap and UNMIRRORED_TOTAL rises to thirteen. Which of the two is the decision this item makes, and the record says why rather than only which. A test then fails when the workspace scan and the classified table disagree, over the whole universe set and not for this one constant, so that the next divergence is caught rather than recounted by hand. That test must name the universe it disagrees about and not merely compare two totals, because two totals that happen to match conceal which row moved. The negative control is confirmed red by restoring the classification the table carries today and watching it fail with DECLARED_RULES named. If the remedy is a real mirror, a second control holds it to being one: it must go red when a rule is added to Registered() and left out of DECLARED_RULES, which is the divergence nothing catches today, and it must be watched failing rather than reasoned about. The module documentation in mirror.rs counts these universes in prose and is wrong either way it lands, so it is corrected as part of this.

items.title: Two items writing different records cannot be independent, because seeding makes them share two files
items.why:
records_do_not_serialize is red at HEAD, and it is red on its own precondition rather than on its subject. Both Test_Two_Items_Writing_Different_Records_Should_Be_Claimable_At_Once and Test_Two_Items_Writing_One_Record_Should_Still_Be_Refused fail at A_Concurrent_Pair with the board must offer two independent record writers. There is no such pair. Five open items reserve a record; every one of them also reserves crates/spec/nomos-spec-store or a parent of it, and every one of them also reserves tests/contract.
This is not an accident of who authored what. OD-LEDGER-001 third authoring rule requires that anything writing a canonical record also reserve crates/spec/nomos-spec-store, because such a record must be seeded in governing.rs with the literal count in governing_records_are_present.rs raised or the workspace goes red. Two items writing two different records must therefore both edit the same two files. They cannot be independent, by construction, and the rule that makes it so was added in the same work as the guarantee it defeats. P10-RECORD-LOCK set out to end exactly this: before it, all nine open items reserved docs/records and the second claim was always refused. Reserving the record instead of the directory removed one edge and left the deeper one in place.
OD-LEDGER-004 already measured it without drawing the conclusion. It lists twenty-two pairs still excluded on genuine code overlap, naming crates/spec and crates/spec/nomos-spec-store at six blocked pairs and tests/contract at five, and treats them as ordinary code contention. What it does not say is that for record-writing items specifically the store overlap is guaranteed by its own authoring rule, so the acceptance test passed at the time only because some pair on the board happened to be disjoint for unrelated reasons. The property was measured true once and is not structurally maintained.
A second global serializer arrived later and independently. P9-PUBLIC-API checks each crate public surface into tests/contract/surface, so any item widening any crate API must update a file under tests/contract, and items are now being widened to reserve that whole directory for the same reason they reserve the store. Two items updating two different snapshot files collide on the directory that holds them, which is the shape P10-RECORD-LOCK named for records, one level up and not yet applied here.
Observed on 2026-08-09. The last concurrent pair existed at 340a310 and went at 91f8159, a widening commit, which by design takes no claim and runs no predicate. No open item predicate builds nomos-ledger except P10-ABANDON-REASON, which is how a red test in nomos-ledger survived several commits with nobody informed - the same shape as a check in a crate the predicate never builds, which is the omission two widening commits on this board have already corrected for themselves.
items.done_when:
The guarantee stops depending on who happens to be on the board. Either two items writing different records can be claimed at once for a structural reason, or the property records_do_not_serialize asserts is restated to one that can actually hold, and which of those it is gets recorded with the reason rather than left to whoever next reads a red suite. Nothing here is closed by editing the guard until it passes, and nothing is closed by narrowing another item territory to manufacture a pair.
If the remedy is structural, the two known collision points are named rather than assumed: the seeding rule, where RECORDS and GOVERNING_RECORD_IDS are hand-maintained lists every record writer must edit, and the surface snapshots, where reserving tests/contract reserves every crate snapshot to write one. Deriving the record list from the directory would remove the first and would also remove a declared universe, which is P10-MIRROR-DISAGREEMENT territory and wants coordinating rather than doing twice.
A test fails when the board serializes again, and it is confirmed red by constructing a board that serializes rather than by reasoning that it would. The file already carries Test_The_Old_Authoring_Should_Offer_No_Concurrent_Pair as the control that the pair search measures exclusion at all; whatever replaces or keeps the acceptance test must still fail against that reconstruction, or the search has stopped measuring anything and the suite reports a success it did not earn. The vacuity guard matters as much: a board with fewer than two open record writers must not pass by having nothing to compare.

items.title: An older binary silently drops the ledger fields it does not know
items.why: Measured on 2026-08-09 rather than inferred. LedgerItem derives Deserialize with no deny_unknown_fields and no schema version, so a nomos.exe built before a field existed reads the current work/ledger.json, ignores the keys it does not know, and writes the document back without them. No error, exit 0. The state change survives and the dropped data does not, so a lossy write is indistinguishable from a successful one at the surface that reports it. The evidence. e88f92d added LedgerItem::abandoned as a Vec<Abandonment> with serde(default) and no skip_serializing_if, so a current binary always emits an empty abandoned list on every item. A round trip through the current binary against a scratch ledger under NOMOS_WORK_DIR confirms that directly: work claim wrote the key to all fifty items and work abandon persisted the reason text verbatim. The repository ledger holds zero such keys. An abandonment of P10-ABANDON-REASON written at unix 1786326402 through a freshly built binary was gone by 1786326839, when another session's work claim rewrote the file - the release stood, the reason did not. This did not start today. Both e88f92d and 6326566 committed a work/ledger.json with zero abandoned keys, including the very commit that added the field, so the authoring session was stripping it as it wrote it and nothing said so. What produced it is the documented Windows workaround rather than carelessness. work finish cannot run under cargo run, because the predicate rebuilds the exe that is the running process, so sessions copy target/debug/nomos.exe and run the copy - and a copy taken before a schema change is a stale writer for the rest of that session. The workaround for a file lock became a silent data loss channel on a file two sessions share. The shape is OD-LEDGER-006 one level down. That record is about a reason attached to a transition not surviving it; this is a reason attached to an item not surviving the next writer, and it fails the same way, by looking like success. The reason destroyed here is worth keeping, because it is the first thing the new field was ever asked to hold: the work was complete and committed at e88f92d, the item's predicate runs -p nomos-ledger which is red on records_do_not_serialize for a cause outside the item, that cause is on the board as P10-SEEDING-SERIALIZES, and the claim reserved the two paths every open item also reserves, so it was refusing the one item able to fix the reason it could not finish.
items.done_when: A write by a binary that does not understand the document it is writing either fails or preserves what it did not understand. Which of those is settled in the record on stated grounds rather than left to whoever implements it: a schema version the writer must recognise, deny_unknown_fields on the way in, or a preserved passthrough of unknown keys. A test asserts it over a document carrying a key the deserializing type does not declare, and asserts on the round tripped document rather than on whether a type compiles. The negative control is confirmed red - removing the guard must fail that test and fail it alone. A second control holds the line the crate already draws: a writer that does understand the document must still round trip it unchanged, because a guard that refuses every write is not a fix and would stop the board rather than protect it. Whether the copied binary workaround is replaced, or only documented so an operator can tell a stale writer from a current one, is settled either way, since a guard that reports only after the loss leaves the operator holding the same problem.

items.title: A lapsed lease invalidates the whole ledger, so one dead agent stops every claim
items.why: Measured on a scratch ledger under NOMOS_WORK_DIR rather than inferred from reading. Document validation in store.rs treats state Claimed with no active claim as a violation - X is marked claimed but has no active claim. A lease expiring is precisely that state, so the moment any lease runs out the whole document stops validating. FileLedger::Claim loads the document before it does anything else and the load validates, so every claim then fails, not only a claim on the lapsed item. Reproduced by forcing one lease into the past and then claiming P9-AUTHORING, which shares no territory with the lapsed item: refused. Meanwhile work list still reports P9-AUTHORING as ready, so the board goes on advertising work nobody can take - the defect P9-DEPENDS-ON closed, reappearing through a different cause. The report also names the wrong thing. Claim writes self.Load().map_err of a closure discarding its argument into ClaimRefusal::NoSuchItem at store.rs:518, so every load failure - an invalid document, an unreadable file, a parse error - is reported as no item named X. The operator is told the identifier is wrong when the ledger is broken. That is why this needed an experiment rather than a glance, and it is a reason attached to a failure not surviving it, the same shape as OD-LEDGER-006 for the third time. Recovery exists, but only for the holder. Renew and Release match on the holder and do not take the validating path, so the agent holding the lapsed claim can renew or abandon it and the board recovers at once. Anyone else is refused: abandoning as another holder is refused with overlaps territory held by dead-agent until unix 1000000000, a lease twenty-five years expired and still excluding. So when the holder is a process that died - which is the only reason a lease ever lapses on its own - nothing on the board can be claimed, renewed or abandoned by anybody, and the only recovery is editing work/ledger.json by hand. MAXIMUM_LEASE exists so that a crashed agent does not hold territory until somebody edits the file, and item.rs says exactly that at the definition of the lapse check. The lease expiring is what causes the thing the lease exists to prevent. The unit level being right is what hid it: Has_Active_Claim returns false on a lapsed claim and its tests pass, and validation refuses the document before exclusion is ever consulted, so the correct answer never gets to matter. This is live rather than theoretical - a four-hour lease was outstanding on this board while it was written.
items.done_when: A lapse behaves the way MAXIMUM_LEASE was introduced to make it behave: an agent that dies holding a claim stops excluding everybody else, and the board keeps working without a human editing the file. What a lapsed claim leaves visible on the item is settled in the record rather than assumed - the crate has already decided a lapse should be distinguishable from work never started, and that decision is not reopened here. A test claims an item, forces its lease into the past, and asserts three things: an unrelated item is still claimable, validate does not call the document invalid, and the lapsed item itself is either claimable or explicitly is not on stated grounds. The negative control is confirmed red and confirmed alone - restoring the violation must fail those tests and nothing else, since a control that reddens the whole suite proves nothing about what it guards. Separately, a load failure names its cause: Claim stops mapping every load error to NoSuchItem, and a test asserts that an invalid document and a genuinely missing item produce different messages, asserting the text itself because the defect is precisely that two causes wore one name.

items.title: work add promises to refuse territory already spoken for, and refuses only a duplicate id
items.why: The doc comment on Add in crates/host/nomos-cli/src/work.rs reads: records a new item, refusing one whose territory is already spoken for. It does not do that. Add rejects a duplicate identifier and then validates the whole document, and the validation that looks at territory overlap only compares against active claims - a brand new item holds no claim, so that check has nothing to say about it and never fires. Demonstrated twice on this board rather than argued. Commits 60d0c5b and 7efc2a9 each added an item reserving crates/substrate/nomos-ledger, crates/spec/nomos-spec-store and tests/contract while another session held all three under an active claim on P10-SEEDING-SERIALIZES, and both were accepted with the message added, reserving 5 paths. Whether Add should refuse is a real question and not obviously yes. Opening an item for work that is currently blocked is the normal way this board is used - both items above were opened precisely because their territory was held - so a refusal would forbid the ordinary case. The likely resolution is that the sentence is wrong rather than the behaviour, but that is a decision to make rather than assume, which is why this reserves a record. What makes it worth an item at all is the class it belongs to. A doc comment asserting a control that does not run is the same defect this ledger has recorded repeatedly under other names - a claim of coverage written where nothing checks it. The next person to reason about whether two items can safely be opened against one territory will read that sentence and be told a check protects them.
items.done_when: The sentence and the behaviour agree, and which one moved is recorded with the reason. If Add is to refuse overlapping territory, a test claims an item and then asserts that adding an overlapping one is refused and names the holder, with the negative control confirmed red alone. If the comment is what was wrong, it says what Add actually guarantees - a unique identifier and a document that still validates - and a test asserts the behaviour the comment now describes, so the correction is held in place by something other than review. Either way the record states why opening an item against held territory is or is not legitimate, since that is the question the sentence was answering wrongly.

items.title: Items reserve the whole snapshot directory to write one file in it
items.why: OD-LEDGER-007 names this as the structural fix and declines to force it, and the debt register it introduced is meant to empty. This is the entry for the second of its two serializers. An item that widens one crate's API must update tests/contract/surface/<crate>.txt, and every such item reserves tests/contract entire - so any two of them exclude each other over files neither will touch. That is exactly the shape OD-LEDGER-004 named when it took docs/records apart: claim the artefact, not the directory. The record directory was merely the most complete instance because every item writes a record; this one is the same defect at the level above, and it was introduced by P9-PUBLIC-API in the same body of work that repaired the first. Nothing in the mechanism prevents the finer grain. Territory is file resolution and Territory::Intersect already compares by containment, so tests/contract/surface/nomos-ledger.txt and tests/contract/surface/nomos-cli.txt are Disjoint today with no code change at all - the same fact that made the record repair possible. What stops it is that four open items belonging to other work reserve the directory, and P10-SEEDING-SERIALIZES explicitly refused to narrow somebody else's territory to manufacture a pair. That refusal was right for that item and is the reason this one exists rather than a reason the work should not happen. Measured on this board rather than asserted: with the record directory already fine-grained and both serializers in place, six probes on 2026-08-09 refused six for six against one claim, and that pattern has now been measured four times in one day under four different holders. items.title: The package seam is declared in contracts, consumed by nothing, and contradicted by publish = false
items.why:
ARCH-001 and ARCH-002 are corpus requirements, not plan preferences. ARCH-001 makes a LanguagePackage "an independently versioned registration and translation boundary for one language ecosystem". ARCH-002 makes a RulePackage "independently versioned" and separates the normative rule contract from its implementations. Both live in the v14 corpus at 01_authoring/artifacts/requirements/ and are restated in volume 03, Packages, Providers, Rules and Applicability. D-132 puts the corpus above the plan, so this is the strongest form the package question has, and neither id appears anywhere in this repository: not in docs/records, not in work/ledger.json, not in source.

Three measurements say the seam is declared and unrealized.

PackageKind in crates/contracts/nomos-contracts/src/package.rs enumerates sixteen kinds and matches the volume's package_kind list variant for variant, LanguagePackage and RulePackage among them. It has zero consumers outside nomos-contracts. That is the shape P10-FIRST-CHECK opened against for enforcement.rs: a published protocol commitment in the one crate whose types nobody compiles, accruing cost.

Cargo.toml line 70 sets publish = false for the whole workspace. Every crate inherits it through publish.workspace = true and carries a hand-written uniform version = "0.1.0". Nothing here is independently versioned or separately distributable, which is the property both requirements are about. The game plan names this exact pattern as a defect to repair, "remove publish = false from genuinely reusable crates, assign meaningful independent or coordinated versions", written about XVPE. This workspace reproduces it.

The two crates the requirements name, crates/languages/nomos-lang-rust and crates/rules/nomos-rules, both sit under crates/ beside the engine and neither can be released on its own.

What this item does not rest on. An earlier reading of this deviation claimed the approved plan required a packages/ directory and rejected a rules crate under crates/. That citation could not be verified. The game plan D-132 names is docs/new docs/nomos full game plan.txt in the code-standards tree, and it contains no lettered sections, no D-084, and no packages path of any kind. Its final revised layout is a flat crates/ holding nomos-checks and nomos-gates, with providers/ as a top-level sibling. So the directory layout is not the finding and is not what this item is about. The versioning property is, and it is measurable at HEAD.
items.done_when: Whether this workspace intends to satisfy ARCH-001 and ARCH-002 is answered and recorded, and the answer names what would have to become true rather than only what is true now. Any of three outcomes closes it: the requirements are accepted and the record states what independently versioned means for a Cargo workspace and what the first step is, or they are deferred and the record states until when and what the deferral costs, or they are read as not reaching this build and the record states why a corpus requirement does not bind the thing built to enforce it. PackageKind either gains a consumer or gains a stated reason for having none, at the site, the way D-134 put a universe's mirror next to the declaration. Nothing here is closed by deleting the enum or by flipping publish, and no crate's publish setting is changed by this item: settling the question is the work, and acting on the answer is a separate item with a much wider territory.

items.title: A lapsed item can only be recovered by the agent that died holding it
items.why: P10-LAPSE-BRICKS stopped a lapse from refusing every claim on the board, and left the lapsed item itself where it was: state Claimed, Claim_Refusal rejects anything that is not Ready, so nobody but the original holder can move it. Renew and Release match on the holder, and the holder is by definition a process that died - that is the only reason a lease ever lapses on its own. So the item is stuck until a person edits work/ledger.json, which is the outcome MAXIMUM_LEASE was introduced to make impossible. OD-LEDGER-009 states why it was not fixed there rather than leaving it to be rediscovered: Claim overwrites claim, and claim is the only thing recording that the work was ever started. OD-LEDGER-006 decided that must survive and refused to synthesize an Abandonment for a lapse, because Abandonment::reason is the words the holder gave and a lapse has none. A takeover therefore has nowhere to put the claim it replaces, and giving it one is a change to what a lapse leaves behind - which is OD-LEDGER-006's decision and was out of scope there. work list now says lapsed rather than claimed, so the stuck item is at least visible; it is not recoverable.
items.done_when: An item whose holder died returns to the pool without a person editing the file, and what happened to it is still readable afterwards. Who held it, when they took it and when the lease ran out survive the takeover - a new claim overwriting the old one silently is the outcome this must not have. Whether that means an Abandonment variant that is not a reason the holder gave, a separate lapsed record on the item, or a takeover operation distinct from claim is the decision, recorded with the criterion rather than chosen by whichever is easiest to write. OD-LEDGER-006 is reopened deliberately or it is not touched. A test claims an item, forces the lease into the past, takes it over as a different holder, and asserts both that the takeover succeeded and that the previous holder is still named on the item. The negative control is confirmed red: a takeover that drops the previous holder must fail it.

items.title: The fact layer has no consumer, and the record that bypassed it argues against filesystems rather than against facts
items.why:
nomos-rules is the only thing in this tree that judges code. Its dependencies are nomos-contracts, nomos-model, syn and proc-macro2. Not nomos-analysis, and not nomos-lang-rust.

FactReader appears in exactly three files, all of them inside crates/substrate/nomos-analysis: the trait at src/reader.rs, the re-export at src/lib.rs, and its own test at tests/fact_identity.rs. There is no consumer anywhere else in the workspace. So P7-ANALYSIS, P7-RUST, P7-SLICE and P8-PIN, and the invalidation and incremental-reuse work behind them, reach nothing that judges. Six closed items of substrate, and the first rule built on top of it consults none of them.

syn appears in two Cargo.toml files: crates/languages/nomos-lang-rust and crates/rules/nomos-rules. One workspace, one language, two independent front ends. D-134 records at length why the second one parses rather than scans and does not record that the first one already exists.

The recorded reason does not reach the conclusion it is attached to. D-134 argues that none of the three OD-COMPLETENESS-001 instances can be replayed from git, and concludes that the only way to judge code that no longer exists is for the rule to accept code as an argument, so the rule takes text. The premise defeats a rule that walks the filesystem. It does not defeat facts. A reader handed in as a parameter is equally an argument, a test can implement it over three files it wrote by hand, and the replay requirement is satisfied identically. Whatever ruled facts out, that is not it.

The decision may still be right. D-134 argues elsewhere that one check honest end to end beats three nearly wired, and scope is a real reason that would carry this. But scope is not the reason recorded, and a record whose argument proves something narrower than its conclusion is what OD-GATE-001 is about, one level in: a claim that implies more than it holds, believed later because it was written down.
items.done_when: The relationship between the rule layer and the fact layer is settled and written down. Either a rule consumes facts and the second syn front end is given a stated reason to remain or is removed, or text stays the rule's subject on grounds that survive the counter above, and in that case the record says what the fact layer is for when no judgment reads it. D-134 is amended or superseded rather than left standing with an argument that does not reach its conclusion, since the argument is the part later work will cite. Not closed by deleting nomos-analysis, and not closed by routing a rule through a fact path that no judgment actually consults, which would satisfy the letter of this item and none of it.

items.title: The guarantee that a judging command cannot report success vacuously is one command remembering, not a type refusing
items.why:
nomos check cannot report a clean run over nothing. An empty walk exits ExitCode::Vacuous, 6, and says so, and the doc comment names the sibling defect it exists against: check-standards-tree /nonexistent walked nothing, found nothing and reported CLEAN. That guard is real, it is tested, and it is better than what it replaces.

It is also entirely local. The enum lives in crates/host/nomos-cli/src/check.rs and is private to that group's module; spec.rs declares its own 6 as Absent. Nothing in nomos-contracts makes a success value unconstructible without evidence that something was judged, so no type stops the next judging group from returning Ok over an empty subject set. The guarantee is one command remembering.

check.rs argues the placement, and argues it well: the guard belongs in the caller "because did I see a plausible amount of the world is a question only the caller that chose the tree can answer". That is a real argument and it is in a doc comment. A cross-command guarantee decided in one module's prose is a decision the next author does not encounter, because the next author reads their own module.

OD-LEDGER-002 already records that nomos-gates, nomos-findings and nomos-applicability do not exist. It does not record how the guarantee those crates were meant to carry is held in their absence. That is the gap here: not the missing crates, which are on the record, but the missing statement of what replaced them and where it now lives.

OD-GATE-001 is this same defect one level out - a skipped test reports ok - and it is closed. This workspace has already decided once that it will not rely on a command remembering to be honest about having run nothing.
items.done_when: Where the no-vacuous-success guarantee lives is decided and recorded rather than argued in a doc comment. Either caller-side placement stands, and the record states what makes the next judging command inherit the guard instead of remembering it - a shared entry point every group routes through, a contract test over every group that can print a verdict, or an explicit acceptance that it is per-command with the cost named and a place it will be noticed. Or the guarantee moves into a value that a judging command cannot construct without having judged something, and the record says what that costs at the seam and what it does not cover. Building nomos-gates is not required to close this, and neither is adding a second judging command: the question is where the property is held, and it can be answered while there is still only one.

items.title: work audit answers for items nobody can act on, by a second guard that disagrees with the first
items.why: P9-DEPENDS-ON closed exactly this defect in work list and did not reach its sibling. Audit at crates/host/nomos-cli/src/work.rs:713 iterates document.items with no state filter, so against the live board it prints 54 lines of which 44 describe Done or Declined items being blocked by a claim they will never contend for. Ten lines describe something actionable and they are not distinguishable by eye. Worse than noise, it is a second implementation of one rule: list goes through Listing_Label, which calls nomos_ledger::Claim_Refusal, while audit calls ExclusionLedger::Conflicts instead, and the doc comment on Claim_Refusal at crates/substrate/nomos-ledger/src/store.rs:436 says in as many words that a second guard for one rule is the thing to avoid. The two already disagree on 44 items. Conflicts is territory-only, so an item refused by DependencyUnmet prints nothing at all and audit cannot say waiting where list can. It also calls Load once per item, parsing the whole ledger 58 times for one command. Finally ClaimRefusal::HeldBy::Describe formats the holders item, so every line reads subject: blocker overlaps territory held by, transposing which of the two names is the subject.
items.done_when: Audit reports only what an agent could act on, and it derives that from the same function list does rather than a second one. Terminal items are absent from the output, not merely sorted below it. An item refused for an unfinished dependency is reported as such, so the command stops being silent about a refusal it cannot express today. The ledger is loaded once per invocation and not once per item. A test pins the output against a board holding a terminal item, a dependency-blocked item and a territory-blocked item at once, and fails if a Done item reappears or if a DependencyUnmet item is dropped; the negative control is that reinstating the unfiltered loop turns it red. Not closed by filtering the printing while leaving Conflicts as a parallel implementation, since the disagreement between two guards is the defect and the line count is only how it was noticed. No new record: OD-LEDGER-005 already states the rule this applies, and citing it is the point.

Twelve is the honest number this item frees once the reservations follow the code out; the rest are held by tests/contract too, which is the other declared serializer and a different items subject. An earlier draft of this why claimed 45 of 45 and 39 of 45, measured when the board had ten writers, and it credited this item with pairs it does not free. The register in records_do_not_serialize.rs is a debt list and OD-LEDGER-007 says it is expected to empty; this is the entry for its remaining half. Three symbols in two files force the collision: RECORDS at src/governing.rs:9, GOVERNING_RECORD_IDS at src/governing.rs:190, and the literal assert_eq on its length at tests/governing_records_are_present.rs:45. items.title: A documented flag makes an item permanently unclaimable and stops every other claim, non-retryably
items.why: work add advertises --territory-pattern in its usage and README documents it beside --territory. Any item carrying one entry in territory.patterns makes Territory::Intersect return Unknown against every other territory - crates/substrate/nomos-ledger/src/territory.rs:130 short-circuits on patterns before comparing a single path - so Refusal_From maps it to UnknownIndependence, whose Is_Retryable is false. The consequences are worse than an item nobody can claim. That item can never be claimed by anyone, its own holder included; every other claim on the board is refused against it; and the refusal tells an agent the independence question is unanswerable, which by the exit-code contract in README means stop and fetch a human rather than try another item. Nothing in work add warns, and validate accepts the document, so a single documented flag bricks the board for every session at once and the failure does not look like contention. Refusing an unanswerable overlap rather than granting it is correct and is the README rule; what is wrong is that the only way to reach that state is an advertised flag for a feature the comparison does not implement. This was found by reading territory.rs while measuring the boards serialization, not by an incident - no open item uses a pattern today, which is why the cost of closing it now is a test and a refusal.
items.done_when: A territory pattern either compares or is refused where it is authored, and it is no longer possible to reach UnknownIndependence through a documented flag. If patterns are refused, work add rejects --territory-pattern with a message naming what is unsupported, the flag leaves the usage text and README, and the refusal is a usage error rather than a ledger error so it cannot be mistaken for contention. If patterns compare, Territory::Intersect answers Disjoint or Overlaps for a pattern against a path and Unknown is reserved for a question the mechanism genuinely cannot answer. Which of the two is the decision this item makes and the record says why, since refusing a flag the README documents is a narrowing of what the ledger offers and OD-LEDGER-001 is the standing statement of what territory promises. A test claims against an item carrying a pattern and pins the outcome, and the negative control is that restoring the unconditional Unknown at territory.rs:130 turns it red. Not closed by leaving the flag in place and documenting the hazard, because the board a documented flag can brick is every sessions board and the warning arrives after the write.

items.title: The three verbs that change the board read and write it without taking the lock the doc comment says they take
items.why: With_Lock at crates/substrate/nomos-ledger/src/store.rs:228 acquires the cross-process lock and its doc comment says every mutation goes through it. Claim, Renew and Release do not. Each does self.Load, mutates the document in memory and calls self.Save with no acquisition anywhere between - Claim at :548 and :568, Renew at :589 and :628, Release at :646 and :688. That is a read-modify-write over a whole-document file, so two sessions interleaving lose one of the two writes entirely, and what is lost is not a field but every change the other session made to any item. This board is worked by several agent sessions at once by design, which is what the lock exists for; the README says two items are concurrently claimable exactly when their territories are disjoint, and that guarantee is enforced by a function the writing path does not call. The failure is silent and looks like the ledger simply not having recorded something. It is close in shape to the loss P10-STALE-WRITER is open for, and is a different cause with the same symptom, which is why it wants separating rather than folding in: a stale binary drops fields it does not know, and this drops changes it never read. Found while designing P10-STALE-WRITER, in territory that item does not need.
items.done_when: Claim, Renew and Release perform their read, their decision and their write inside one lock acquisition, or the doc comment on With_Lock stops claiming they do and the record says why an unlocked read-modify-write is acceptable for these three and not for the paths that already use it. A test drives two concurrent writers against one ledger and fails if either write is lost - not two sequential calls, since sequential calls cannot reproduce it. The negative control is that removing the acquisition again makes that test red. Whether the lock is taken by moving these three onto With_Lock or by another means is the decision, and it must account for finish, which runs a predicate that can take minutes and must not hold a cross-process lock while it does. Not closed by documenting the race, and not closed by a test that only proves the lock can be acquired.

items.title: A record reservation is disjoint from the record it reserves, so amending an existing one excludes nobody
items.why: OD-LEDGER-001s third authoring rule tells an item to reserve the record identifier it will allocate, docs/records/OD-AREA-NNN, and P10-RECORD-LOCK re-authored every open item that way to stop the record directory serializing the board. It works for the case it was designed for - two items reserving the same identifier collide, because the two paths are equal - and it silently reserves nothing against the file. Containment is right.starts_with of left plus a slash at crates/substrate/nomos-ledger/src/territory.rs:230, so docs/records/OD-LEDGER-006 and docs/records/OD-LEDGER-006-a-reason-attached-to-a-transition-does-not-survive-it.md are siblings and compare Disjoint. An item amending an existing record therefore excludes nobody from the file it edits unless it happens to spell the whole filename, and the two spellings do not exclude each other either. Every open item on this board reserves a stem. The guard cannot see it: Test_A_Record_Should_Exclude_Nobody_But_Its_Own_Writer reduces items to their record paths and claims them, which stems do correctly, so the property it measures is true of stems and says nothing about files. Found while designing P10-LAPSE-TAKEOVER, which must amend two records that already exist and discovered that reserving their identifiers reserved neither.
items.done_when: Reserving a records identifier excludes an item that will write that records file, and the two spellings of one record collide. Either containment learns that docs/records/OD-AREA-NNN covers docs/records/OD-AREA-NNN-<slug>.md, which is a change to what territory means and must say why a stem is a prefix of a name rather than of a path, or OD-LEDGER-001s rule requires the full filename once the file exists and the identifier only before it does, and something checks that rather than the author remembering. Whichever is chosen, the open items that amend an existing record are re-authored to match, and only while unclaimed. A test asserts the two spellings collide and names both; the negative control is that restoring the current comparison turns it red. The record states what P10-RECORD-LOCK actually bought, since the property it claimed is true of identifiers and was read as true of records. Not closed by re-authoring the items and leaving the comparison as it is, because the next item to amend a record will spell it the same wrong way.

items.title: Blanking a test module blanks whatever braced item follows a brace-less one
items.why: Without_Test_Modules at tests/contract/src/gates.rs:708 finds a cfg(test) marker and then blanks from it to Next_Code_Byte for an open brace, with no bound on how far that search runs. For an item that has a body the brace it finds is that items own. For a brace-less one - cfg(test) mod name; is the ordinary way to declare a test-only module in another file - the next brace in the file belongs to some later, unrelated item, and everything between them is blanked including that item. Found by P10-SEED-GRAIN: adding cfg(test) mod registration; among the mod lines of nomos-spec-store swallowed the pub use that followed it, and Test_Every_Crates_Public_Surface_Should_Match_Its_Snapshot went red reporting eleven missing exports and a re-export it could not resolve. Nothing pointed at the scanner; the failure names the crate whose surface moved. That item worked around it by putting the declaration last in lib.rs with a comment, because tests/contract was not in its territory, so the workaround is load-bearing and undocumented outside one comment. The scanner is wrong for any crate that declares a test module this way, and the public surface snapshot is what silently changes.
items.done_when: A brace-less cfg(test) item blanks itself and nothing after it, and a cfg(test) item with a body still blanks its whole body. The search for a body is bounded by the end of the item it belongs to rather than by the end of the file, so a declaration ending in a semicolon is recognised as having no body rather than borrowing the next one. Unit tests in tests/contract/src/gates.rs cover both forms and the interaction that was actually observed - a brace-less declaration followed by a braced item, asserting the following item survives - and the negative control is that restoring the unbounded search turns them red while naming the item that was eaten. The workaround left in crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/src/lib.rs is removed and its comment with it, so the declaration order stops being load-bearing; if it is kept the item says why. No new record: this is a scanner defect rather than a decision, and OD-GATE-002 already states what the surface check is for.

items.title: One payload schema, two encoders, three readers, and no written grammar
items.why: nomos.syntax.items.v1 is a SchemaId string in nomos-cap-syntax and nothing else. nomos-lang-rust::Encode_Payload and nomos-lang-rust-scan each author the bytes independently, and three consumers read them back: tests/integration/src/surface.rs, crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/facts.rs, and whoever is next. The contract crate exists because an agreement is not the property of one party to it, and the shape of the answer is the part of that agreement with no home. Two encoders that drift produce facts that decode differently under one capability, and nothing in the tree would notice. Separately, the payload cannot distinguish a trait-method signature from a function definition except by an incidental encoding of visibility, which nomos-rules now depends on and OD-RULES-001 wrote down as a shape convention rather than a guarantee.
items.done_when: The grammar of nomos.syntax.items.v1 is written down in nomos-cap-syntax, where both parties can name it, together with one reader or one writer that the tree agrees is canonical. Every consumer either uses it or has a stated reason not to. The trait-signature distinction is either something the schema states or something the schema explicitly declines to state, in writing. Not closed by documenting the current bytes in a comment, and not closed by promoting a reader nobody but its author calls.

items.title: A payload that carries what a provider did not observe, so the second syn front end can go
items.why: SyntaxItem carries no doc comment and no declared type, so universe discovery cannot be served from facts and nomos-rules keeps a syn front end for exactly that. OD-RULES-001 measured this and gave the residual parser a stated reason and this item as its end condition; without this item the exception has no expiry and becomes a habit. Adding the two fields is not a field addition. nomos-lang-rust-scan cannot read doc comments at all: it skips comment lines and associates nothing with the item below them, so a schema in which this item has no doc comment and this provider does not read doc comments are the same bytes turns every universe under the scanner into one declaring no mirror. That is a phantom mirror silently downgraded to an admitted gap, which is absence becoming success in the one field the completeness-mirror rule severity ordering turns on.
items.done_when: A version of the syntax payload carries, per item, what each provider actually observed about its documentation and its declared type shape, bounded by that provider guarantee, so that not observed and not present are different bytes. nomos-rules/src/universe.rs reads facts, and syn and proc-macro2 leave crates/rules/nomos-rules/Cargo.toml. A test proves that a universe read through the scanner is not reported as an admitted gap. Not closed by adding two optional fields that a provider which cannot fill them leaves empty.

items.title: Three normalizations of a path into a subject, and the note that said the third one settles it
items.why: nomos_ledger::Subject_Of, tests/integration/src/corpus.rs::Subject_Of_Path and now crates/host/nomos-cli/src/check.rs each reduce a path to a SubjectId by nearly the same rules. corpus.rs states in its own doc comment that the duplication is worth converging behind one home the moment a third caller appears, and OD-RULES-001 made that third caller. They are not identical: the ledger folds a record filename onto its record identifier and the other two do not, so converging is a decision about whether a claim and a fact address the same thing rather than a move of one function. Left as it is, two of the three drift and a composition root files facts under subjects a rule computes differently, which reads as every fact being unavailable rather than as one function being wrong.
items.done_when: Either the three normalizations become one, with the record-filename fold expressed as something the caller asks for rather than as a difference between two copies, or the tree records why a subject for a claim and a subject for a fact are deliberately different things and each copy names that reason at its site. Not closed by importing one of the three into the other two without settling which question they answer.

items.title: Blessing one crates surface rewrites every crates surface, so a concurrent worker loses its own
items.why: tests/contract/tests/public_surface.rs:15 says the variable rewrites every snapshot, and it does. That is harmless for one author working alone and wrong for this tree, which is worked by several agent sessions at once by design and says so in README. Observed on 2026-08-09 between two live claims: the holder of P10-FACT-BYPASS blessed to update tests/contract/surface/nomos-rules.txt, which rewrote the three snapshots the holder of P10-SPEC-DETERMINISM had deliberately changed and not yet committed; that holder reverted the three foreign files, and the other holder found its own work silently reverted mid-lease and re-applied it by hand. Both behaved correctly and the data survived because a human-shaped agent noticed. Nothing in the mechanism noticed. The failure mode is worse than it looks: blessing rewrites a snapshot to whatever the current tree exports, so a foreign snapshot carrying an uncommitted change is not merely reverted to HEAD but rewritten from a half-finished tree, and the result still passes the surface test. It is territory violation by a tool rather than by an author, and territory cannot express it because the writer is a test the other worker also has to run.
items.done_when: Blessing writes only the snapshots the blesser asked for. The variable names what to rewrite - a crate, or a list of them - and naming nothing rewrites nothing rather than rewriting everything, so the widest possible action is not the easiest one to reach for. The deliberate failure after a bless stays, because a bless that passes is a check anybody can switch off, and that reasoning is unchanged. A test asserts that blessing one crate leaves another crates snapshot byte-identical, including when that other snapshot disagrees with the tree - which is the case that actually bit, and the negative control is that restoring the rewrite-everything behaviour turns it red. The doc comment at the top of the file stops saying every snapshot. No new record: OD-GATE-002 already states what the surface check is for and this does not change it.

items.title: Four package kinds carry a suffix the corpus taxonomy does not, and the label is what a peer reimplements
items.why: Found by P10-PACKAGE-SEAM and recorded in OD-PACKAGE-001 rather than fixed, because renaming a protocol surface was outside a versioning items done_when. The game plan carries three copies of the package taxonomy and they disagree: two match volume 03s sixteen kinds exactly, the third omits RepositoryProvider and suffixes four names. PackageKind follows the third and extends its suffix to the member that copy was missing, so ToolProviderPackage, MetricProviderPackage, RepositoryProviderPackage and RuntimeProviderPackage diverge from the corpus. D-132 puts the corpus above the plan, so the copy this enum followed is the one with the least authority of the three. This is not a naming preference. PackageKind::Label is the serialized form, and nomos-contracts is deliberately dependency-free because non-Rust peers reimplement it - so the label is a protocol commitment to those peers and a divergent label is a divergent wire format, not a local identifier. It is cheapest to correct now: no code outside the crate names PackageKind, so there is nothing to migrate, and the first consumer will pin whatever is there when it arrives.
items.done_when: The kinds this workspace declares are the kinds the corpus names, or each difference has a stated reason at the site naming which authority it follows and why. Volume 03 and the two agreeing plan copies are read directly and quoted in the record with resolved paths, since this repository has been bitten by citations that do not resolve, and the third copy is named as the one that was followed. If the corpus and the plan disagree about a kind, D-132 settles it and the record says so rather than choosing quietly. A test asserts every declared kind and its label against the enumeration the record fixes, so a seventeenth kind or a relabelled one cannot arrive without moving the assertion, and the negative control is that renaming one label back turns it red naming the kind. tests/contract/surface/nomos-contracts.txt moves with any rename and is re-blessed deliberately. Not closed by renaming the variants and leaving Label alone, since the label is the half a peer actually reads, and not closed by adding a consumer - PackageKind having none is OD-PACKAGE-001s subject and stays open there.

items.title: One unreadable fixture makes every phantom advisory, so the guard D-134 says must block cannot block
items.why: Found by P10-MIRROR-DISAGREEMENTs eighth negative control and measured, not inferred: renaming a universes claimed mirror to a name that resolves to nothing produced [Advisory] ... resolves to no check ... and the check index is incomplete, because 1 subject(s) could not be read, and nomos check exited 0. D-134 decision 4 stands at version 2 and says a false claim of coverage blocks while an admitted gap is advisory. In this tree neither half can fire for a phantom, because tests/corpus/analysis/gamma/broken.rs is a deliberately unparseable fixture that nomos-lang-rust refuses, so index.Incompleteness() is Some for every run over this workspace and every phantom is downgraded. The downgrade itself is right and OD-RULES-001 argues for it correctly: a rule must not manufacture a phantom out of its own inability to look, and absence must become neither success nor failure. What is wrong is its scope. Incompleteness is global, so one unreadable subject anywhere silences a phantom claimed in a file whose facts were read perfectly well, and the two facts have nothing to do with each other. The result is a guard that reports rather than judges, permanently, and the workspace contradicts a standing governing decision while every test is green.
items.done_when: A phantom in a subject whose facts were read blocks, whatever some other subject did.
